title: The child dies (2 Samuel 12:15–23)
hookLine: David fasts while the child lives, then rises and eats: "I shall go to him"

cards: The servants are whispering in the hallway, and that is how the king finds out. Night after night he has lain on the ground, refusing to eat, even when the elders of his house tried to lift him up.
Now the child is gone, and nobody wants to say it. If he was like this while the boy lived, they ask each other, what will he do when he hears? David sees them whispering.
Is the child dead? And they say: he is dead.

teach.h: THE CHILD IS STRUCK. IT STAYS HARD.
teach.b: This part of the chapter opens with a hard sentence: the Lord struck the child, and he was very sick. It's fair to let that line stay hard. The child did nothing, and the text doesn't explain it away.
While the boy lived, David pleaded with God for him, fasted, and lay on the earth. On the seventh day the child died. Then the surprise.
David gets up from the ground.
He washes, anoints himself, changes his clothes, goes into the house of the Lord and bows down. Then he comes home, asks for food, and eats.
His servants can't make sense of it: you wept while he lived, and now you rise and eat? His answer is plain. While the child was alive I fasted and wept, because who knows?
Maybe God would be gracious, and the child would live. Now he is dead. Why should I fast?
Can I bring him back again?
"I shall go to him," he says, but he will not return to me. Some hear only the grave in that line: everyone will one day go where the child has gone. Some hear a quiet hope of meeting again.
The text doesn't decide. What it shows is a turn.

teach.h: FIGHT WHILE IT CAN CHANGE. THEN RISE.
teach.b: While something could still change, David fought for it with everything he had. When it couldn't, he stopped fighting it and went on living. That isn't the same as not caring.
The man who rises and eats is the same man who lay on the ground all night.

how: In Jewish mourning, people grieve fully and then, step by step, return to ordinary life; David's rising and eating after the child's death is sometimes taught alongside those customs, though the customs come from later law.

o: leaving the palace to mourn in the field
giving up hope while the child still lived
rising from grief to wash, eat and go on

games.q: the child dies — tap the pairs.
p: David fasted and lay on the earth
tried to lift him from the ground

s: David fasted after the child died
he fasted while the child lived; afterward he washed, worshiped, and ate.
David saw the servants whispering and asked
is the child dead? and they said, he is dead.
the text explains why the child had to die

games.q: you're one of David's servants. the child has died, and the king hasn't eaten for days. what do you do?
o: hold back and whisper with the others.
bring him food and say nothing.
games.why: they were afraid to tell him and whispered among themselves; David saw it and asked them himself.

practice: Let something come to mind that you keep pushing against: a loss, a door that has closed. If something is left to do, set it aside for later; if nothing is, let your hands open on your lap and breathe out slowly.
If you pray, you can place it before God.

wordCard.voice: Gets up. What David did after days of fasting and grief, before he washed, ate, and went on living. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: I am going to him, from David's answer in 2 Samuel 12:23.

carryVoice: Your line: I shall go to him. Looking back on the week: lament, b'chol oz, chesed, Bathsheba, parable, chatati, and gets up. That's day seven hundred forty-nine.
